# Step 1: Scope

## Introduction

Decide what your [ontology](../../../docs/GLOSSARY.md#concept-ontology) is for, and write down the questions it must answer.

Without this, you can't tell when you're done. An ontology about "wine" can grow forever. An ontology that must answer six specific questions has an end. What it covers, and what it leaves out, is its [scope](../../../docs/GLOSSARY.md#concept-scope). You can read the full guide to this step in [Methodology](../../../docs/METHOD.md#step-1-scope).

## What you'll make

A written scope (domain, purpose, users, what's left out) and six competency questions. A [competency question](../../../docs/GLOSSARY.md#concept-competency-question) is a question your ontology should be able to answer. You'll use them to test your work in step 8.

## Run the commands

Set the scope first. The Ontology 101 example covers wines, foods and which pairings are good. Winery inventory and restaurant staff are out:

```bash
okb scope --domain "Wines, foods, and which wines go well with which foods" --purpose "Suggest good wine and food combinations for a restaurant menu and answer diners' questions" --users diners,waiters --maintainers sommelier --out-of-scope "winery inventory" --out-of-scope "restaurant staff"
```

```text
Wine and Food
  domain        Wines, foods, and which wines go well with which foods
  purpose       Suggest good wine and food combinations for a restaurant menu and answer diners' questions
  users         diners, waiters
  maintainers   sommelier
  out of scope  winery inventory, restaurant staff
  kind          application
```

Now add the questions. Write each one the way a diner or a waiter would ask it:

```bash
okb cq add "Which wine characteristics should I consider when choosing a wine?"
okb cq add "Is Bordeaux a red or white wine?"
okb cq add "Does Cabernet Sauvignon go well with seafood?"
okb cq add "What is the best choice of wine for grilled meat?"
okb cq add "Which characteristics of a wine affect its appropriateness for a dish?"
okb cq add "Which wines does a given winery produce?"
```

```text
Added cq.1.

Added cq.2.

Added cq.3.

Added cq.4.

Added cq.5.

Added cq.6.
```

## Read the output

- okb numbers each question (`cq.1`, `cq.2` and so on). You'll use those numbers in step 8 to link each question to the parts of the ontology that answer it.
- The out-of-scope list matters as much as the scope. When someone asks "is the vintage year in scope?" later, you can point at the list.
- Look at what the questions ask for. They're [competency questions](../../../docs/learn/competency-questions.md), and each one names a part the ontology needs. "Is Bordeaux a red or white wine?" needs a [class](../../../docs/GLOSSARY.md#concept-class) called Bordeaux. "Which wines does a winery produce?" needs a link between wines and wineries. The questions already hint at the model.

## Check your work

`okb status` shows each step and what it still needs:

```bash
okb status
```

```text
Wine and Food  · 0 classes · 0 slots · 0 instances · 6 questions

✓ 1. Determine the domain and scope ◀ you are here
     ✓ Domain and purpose are written down
     ✓ Users (and ideally maintainers) are named
     ✓ At least three competency questions
     ✓ At least one thing is explicitly out of scope
○ 2. Consider reusing existing ontologies
○ 3. Enumerate important terms
○ 4. Define the classes and the class hierarchy
○ 5. Define the properties of classes (slots)
○ 6. Define the facets of the slots
○ 7. Create instances
○ 8. Review against your questions, and iterate

Validator (steps 1–1): ✗ 0  ! 0  i 0   okb validate for details

Step 1 looks done. When you're happy with it: okb step next
```

Step 1 has four checks, and all of them have a tick. When you see "Step 1 looks done", move on. This prints the guide for step 2:

```bash
okb step next
```

```text
Now on step 2. (To read a step's guide without moving: okb explain 2)

Step 2 of 8: Consider reusing existing ontologies

  Goal: Check whether someone has already modeled part of your domain, and decide whether to
  borrow, adapt, just reference it, or skip it.
  Why it matters: Reuse saves time and makes your ontology compatible with others. If you have
  to talk to systems that already use a vocabulary, reuse may not be optional.

Questions to answer
  • Is there an industry standard, taxonomy or controlled vocabulary for this domain?
  • Does any system you must integrate with already use a particular vocabulary?
  • Is there an internal list, spreadsheet, glossary or schema that already names these things?

You're done when
  ○ Reuse has been considered and recorded

Tips
  • Even a glossary page or an existing database schema counts as a source of terms.
  • Don't let this step stall you. 30 minutes of looking is usually enough for a first version.
  • Where to look: Linked Open Vocabularies (https://lov.linkeddata.es) searches hundreds of
  reusable vocabularies by term. schema.org (https://schema.org) covers everyday things: people,
  organizations, products, places, events and creative works.
  • W3C vocabularies cover common needs: SKOS for taxonomies and thesauri, Dublin Core for
  document metadata, PROV-O for provenance, ORG for organizations and OWL-Time for dates and
  times.
  • For design systems: WAI-ARIA roles (https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria/) are a standard taxonomy
  of UI components (button, checkbox, switch, tab...). The W3C Design Tokens format
  (https://www.designtokens.org) is the standard for tokens. DSDS, the Design System
  Documentation Spec (https://designsystemdocspec.org), is a draft schema for documenting
  components, tokens and themes.
  • You rarely need to import a whole vocabulary. Borrowing its terms and definitions is usually
  enough.

In Ontology 101's wine example
  Ontology 101 notes a French-wine knowledge base or a wine retailer's list of wine properties
  could be imported, but chooses to build from scratch for teaching purposes.

Commands
  okb reuse add   okb reuse none
```

> **Common mistakes**
>
> - **Fewer than three questions.** okb asks for at least three, because one or two don't test much.
> - **Questions that are really tasks.** "Build a menu" isn't a competency question. "Which wine goes with this dish?" is.
> - **No out-of-scope list.** Without it, every idea seems to belong.

## Next step

You wrote down what the ontology is for and six questions it must answer. Next, you'll check whether anyone has already modeled wine, so you don't start from scratch.
